text:
maria: Heads up — saw a chunk of ALB targets in eu-west1 get deregistered after a node failover. Happened ~18:23 UTC. Health checks started failing for pods on node-pool-b for ~45s. No 5xx in app logs. Any theories?

devon: Which healthcheck path and target type are we using (ip vs instance)? Can you paste a sample ALB access log line and a curl from the node to the pod?

maria: Health path is /healthz (GET). Target type is ip. Quick curl from the failing node: 

```
$ curl -sv http://10.244.3.12:8080/healthz
* Connected to 10.244.3.12 (10.244.3.12) port 8080 (#0)
> GET /healthz HTTP/1.1
> Host: 10.244.3.12
> User-Agent: curl/7.64.1
> Accept: */*
\n< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Type: application/json
< Content-Length: 27
{ "status": "ok" }
```

But ALB logs show the target response code 504 and "connect timeout" for those same pod IPs. kubectl get endpoints svc/edge-svc shows endpoints present.

anika: Seen something similar before — when a node's SNAT mapping moves (node reboot / failover) we occasionally see ALB healthchecks time out because conntrack on the node still maps the flow to the old underlying socket. Can you dump the nat table POSTROUTING rules?

maria: Posted iptables nat rules from the node below: 

```
$ iptables -t nat -S | grep MASQUERADE
-A POSTROUTING -s 10.244.0.0/16 -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE --random-fully
```

maria: ALB logs show health requests coming from 10.1.2.5 then 10.1.3.6 (ALB health IPs). conntrack on the node has established entries to 10.244.3.12:8080 but with a source port that got reused after the node came back.

devon: That fits conntrack port reuse/asymmetric SNAT. If the node was recycled quickly the NAT tuple can collide and replies go to the wrong process/socket. Check `conntrack -L | grep 10.244.3.12` and look for very short timeouts. Also what's kube-proxy mode (iptables vs ipvs)?

maria: kube-proxy is iptables mode on this cluster. Conntrack dump shows lots of TIME_WAIT entries and a few ESTABLISHED with low timeout.

anika: Short-term workaround: restart kube-proxy or flush conntrack entries for the affected pod IPs. Longer-term: consider disabling SNAT for the ALB on node egress (externalTrafficPolicy: Local on the service) or switch ALB to target type "instance" so healthchecks hit node IPs where kube-proxy will forward correctly.
tim: Another option — enable preserve client IP for the service so backend sees the real source and doesn't rely on SNAT mapping, but that requires adjustments to route tables/security. Worth a follow-up.
srebot: deploy-bot: scaled node-pool-b from 1 -> 3 at 1749130200 to reduce churn (automated).

maria: We tried a kube-proxy restart + conntrack flush on the two affected nodes and ALB re-registered the pods after ~2 minutes. No app errors.

devon: Action items: 1) add a postmortem blurb explaining SNAT/conntrack risk during fast node failovers, 2) evaluate service.externalTrafficPolicy=Local for edge-svc in eu-west1, 3) consider ALB target type switch to instance or add ALB IP allowlist and hostNetwork health endpoint.
anika: I'll open a follow-up ticket to test externalTrafficPolicy change in staging and measure any impact on IP consumption.
tim: Also let's add a short runbook for conntrack flush + kube-proxy restart for on-call to follow when ALB target deregistration spikes.
maria: thanks — will draft the runbook and link logs. Closing the thread after tickets created.
